issues.legal_issue: An environmental tribunal cannot summarily dismiss a claim concerning the unlawful allotment of village water bodies without adjudicating the dispute on its merits.
material_facts: The tribunal dismissed the application after relying on an authority’s representation that a larger alternative water body was being developed, without considering the merits or the full scope of the applicant’s claims.
The representation relied on to dismiss the application was filed after the tribunal had issued its order.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the tribunal’s order and allowed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22 of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 makes an appeal akin to a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, limiting the Court’s deliberation to a substantial question of law. The Court set aside the tribunal’s summary disposition after addressing the substantive legality of the allotments.

predicates.appeal_from_environmental_tribunal: A party brought an appeal from an environmental tribunal’s decision.
predicates.tribunal_dismissed_without_merits: The tribunal dismissed the application without adjudicating the dispute on its merits.
predicates.dismissal_relied_on_unadjudicated_altern: The tribunal relied on a proposed alternative measure that had not been adjudicated in the proceedings.

issues.definition: When an environmental tribunal appeal concerns a dismissal without a merits decision based on an unadjudicated alternative, the tribunal’s order is set aside.

issues.legal_issue: Common village water bodies cannot be allotted to private industrial interests, and their destruction cannot be justified merely by creating replacement water bodies elsewhere.
material_facts: Revenue records identified the disputed lands as ponds or canals, and the ponds had been used by local villagers as common resources.
The authority allotted water-body land to a private industrial entity and began filling ponds while proposing to develop a larger alternative water body elsewhere.
The proposed industrial use was not shown to be an extraordinary circumstance serving a social public purpose or benefiting the local community.
The original water bodies supported local people, groundwater, vegetation, and wildlife, and the proposed replacement could not ensure that these effects would be offset.
issues.conclusion: The allotments of the water bodies to the private entity or similar third parties were illegal and were quashed; the State’s scheme allowing destruction of water bodies in exchange for alternatives was impermissible.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 21 of the Constitution, community resources such as ponds must be protected as part of the right to a healthy environment. Articles 48A and 51A(g) support the State’s environmental duties. Hinch Lal Tiwari v. Kamala Devi, (2001) 6 SCC 496, holds that ponds are public utilities for common use and cannot be allotted or commercialised. Jagpal Singh v. State of Punjab, (2011) 11 SCC 396, establishes the inalienability of common lands subject to limited exceptions, including certain uses for the downtrodden or public utilities. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (1988) 1 SCC 471, is relied on concerning environmental duties. A geographically larger replacement water body does not ensure that the ecological and community effects of destroying the original will be offset.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_village_water_bodies and land_is_a_common_water_body and allotment_is_for_private_industry and no_qualifying_public_purpose_exception and replacement_water_body_is_offered

predicates.appeal_concerning_village_water_bodies: A party brought an appeal concerning water bodies used as village commons.
predicates.land_is_a_common_water_body: The land was identified or used as a pond, canal, or other common water body.
predicates.allotment_is_for_private_industry: A public authority allotted the water-body land for private industrial use.
predicates.no_qualifying_public_purpose_exception: The proposed use was not shown to fall within a limited exception serving a qualifying public purpose or benefiting the downtrodden.
predicates.replacement_water_body_is_offered: The authority proposed to destroy the original water body while providing a replacement elsewhere.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns a village common water body allotted for private industry without a qualifying public-purpose exception, offering a replacement does not make the allotment lawful.

issues.legal_issue: A change in the statutory vesting of village common land does not by itself alter the land’s character or extinguish established community rights.
material_facts: The ponds and canals were recorded as common lands and had long been used by local people.
A respondent argued that repeal of the earlier land law and vesting of the land in the State ended the community’s rights.
The Court found that the change in statutory vesting did not alter the land’s character contrary to the revenue records or defeat long-established rights.
issues.conclusion: The repeal and transfer of title to the State did not extinguish the local community’s established rights in the common water bodies.
issues.legal_principle: Relying on Chigurupati Venkata Subbayya v. Palaguda Anjayya, (1972) 1 SCC 521, the Court held that the transfer of land to the Government, even where a law extinguishes rights created by former landholders, does not necessarily extinguish community rights that originated independently. The repeal of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 and the vesting provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Revenue Code, 2006 did not change the land’s character or defeat established communal rights.

predicates.appeal_concerning_village_commons: A party brought an appeal concerning land used as a village common.
predicates.land_has_longstanding_community_use: Local people had established community use of the land over a long period.
predicates.statutory_change_transfers_title_to_stat: A statutory change transferred title to the land to the State.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns village common land with long-standing community use, a statutory transfer of title to the State does not by itself extinguish the community’s rights.
